title: Alert on the last five minutes
hook: A service emits timestamped error events. An alert must show the number in the last five minutes after each new event.
context: Monitoring pipeline with events arriving in timestamp order
solution_brief: Keep a deque of timestamps inside the rolling interval. Append each new event and pop expired timestamps from the front. Each event is appended and removed at most once: O(1) amortized update, O(W) memory for W live events. An unsorted array scan costs O(N) per update; a heap adds O(log N) work that ordered arrivals do not need.

steps.prompt: Which structure supports adding a new timestamp and evicting the oldest?

options.text: An unsorted array with full scans

steps.explanation: A supports append and front removal. B rescans history per event. C does not model a rolling window.
steps.bottleneck_note: Ordered input lets the oldest expired event sit at the front.

steps.prompt: At timestamp t, which entries should be removed for a strict trailing 300-second interval (t-300, t]?

options.text: Entries with timestamp less than or equal to t-300

steps.explanation: A matches the open lower bound. B keeps old events. C empties the useful window.
steps.bottleneck_note: Boundary choice matters at exactly five minutes.
steps.context_note: The monitoring contract excludes events exactly 300 seconds old.

steps.prompt: A burst expires many entries at once. What is amortized work per event over the stream?
steps.explanation: A holds because each event is inserted once and removed once. B charges a full history scan to every event. C assumes sorting that ordered input avoids.
steps.bottleneck_note: A single slow eviction does not change the total linear work.
steps.context_note: The deque has already been maintained since startup.

steps.prompt: What changes if events arrive out of timestamp order?

options.text: The front may no longer be the oldest; reorder within a bounded lateness window or use a time index
Nothing; deque order is always timestamp order
Discard every event until the clock catches up

steps.explanation: A names the broken invariant and a recovery. B confuses arrival with event time. C loses valid late events.
steps.bottleneck_note: Document whether the window uses event time or arrival time.
steps.context_note: A network delay makes an older event arrive after a newer one.

steps.prompt: A long quiet period follows a burst. When does the displayed count reach zero?

options.text: On a clock tick or read that evicts expired entries, even without a new event
Only when the next error arrives
Never; old timestamps stay in the deque forever

steps.explanation: A maintains a truthful live count. B displays stale alerts through quiet periods. C ignores expiry entirely.
steps.bottleneck_note: An event-only update loop needs a timer or read-time eviction.
steps.context_note: The UI must update while no errors arrive.
